What is the use of sending [them away]? If their latent consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) remains obstructed, it cannot yet be permitted to dispel demonic activities. Examine and contemplate carefully what is shown in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Question: An ancient said, "The Buddha is the sun. To describe the Buddha-nature, he said: "It is like the bright sun shining in the sky. To describe the Buddha...
Regarding "light," it is also said to be like a hundred thousand suns; this is established based on the visualization of the sun. Unless one is born blind, there is no one who does not see the sun.

This is because the visualization of the mind is easily accomplished, yet various masters have abandoned this and instead rely on the visualization of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-tuft between the brows).

I suspect they have thereby confused and disordered the sequence of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. Some may argue that they fear [this method] would be conflated with those who absorb the essence of the sun.

[The opponent asks: "You alone do not consider the discourse on the yellow palaces between the eyebrows, nor the theory of the gate and the hall; does this not conflate my Middle Way [view]? [The respondent] answers:

"To observe the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-tuft) without observing the solar disc (*sūrya-maṇḍala*) is to proceed by skipping stages; there is indeed a specific reason for this. It is truly because one observes..."

Although the gateways are vast, when one designates the Great Lord, the mention of the Buddha alone suffices. Although the marks of the Buddha are numerous, when one expresses the Middle Way, the single tuft of hair between the brows serves as the unifying principle.
This is indeed established for those who delight in simplicity and convenience while being weary of complexity and elaboration.

It may appear as though this violates the proper sequence; yet in truth, it does no harm. I am merely lamenting that whenever a teaching is established, Māra follows suit, and there are instances beyond count where the heterodox is mixed with the orthodox.
Alas! Not only do they misinterpret the scriptural texts, but they further allow these errors to flow into worldly harm.

They inhale the sun and moon while harboring demons to bring about their own destruction; they guard the *indranīla* (forehead) point while accumulating fiery heat to blind themselves. This is oppressive...

Qi stagnates at the navel and becomes *gǔ* (internal parasites); it courses through the *rèn* and *dū* channels and forms carbuncles and abscesses. Calamity reaches the virtuous people, and misfortune is passed down to future generations. Is this not tragic?
Question: One might fear that the absence of women in the Pure Land could confuse practitioners;

yet, Avalokiteśvara emerges from the Pure Land and frequently manifests as a woman, such as the one known as the "Horse-herder’s Wife" (Mālang-fu) and others mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Questions of Mañjuśrī*, or the young girl encountered by Sudhana in the *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*.
These are all manifestations of compassion. For Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) begin their practice of compassionate deliverance precisely through such means.

It is simply a person. Since the Buddha’s mind is fundamentally compassionate, why is it that when he returns to his original land, he manifests majestic light rather than a compassionate countenance?

Answer: Because the defilements of desire are particularly heavy in Sahā, Avalokiteśvara appears as a woman to transform their minds. This is a skillful means (upāya) distinct from [the case of] Sudhana.
This was not yet understood; therefore, Vāsukī manifested as a woman to communicate her wisdom. This was not what is meant by compassionate transformation (*maitrī-vinaya*).

To manifest as a woman while practicing compassion means that before compassion has been exercised, the fires of lust have already blazed up. For a noble youth of the Nine Lotuses who has only recently begun to cultivate a pure mind, for a woman to damage the sprout of his goodness would be most inappropriate.
Question: Regarding the Dharma-ending age, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* was to perish first, while the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* remained longer.
Now, the one sought to be seen through the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* is this very Amitābha; the one sought to be seen through the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* is likewise this very Amitābha.
It is said that constant practice is difficult, and thus achieving contemplation is also difficult; it is said that seeing the Buddha standing before one is difficult.
Yet those who practice contemplation today consider even the daily contemplation difficult to achieve, and instead focus directly on the white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā*).
How could a contemplation that is difficult to achieve today become easier to perform at the time when the Dharma is extinguished?
Answer: The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* that remains further in the world is the *Great Amitābha Sūtra*, not the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations*.

This is because the invocation of the name is easy to perform, whereas visualization and contemplation are difficult to accomplish. The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* first contemplates the wheel of the feet and proceeds upward through reverse order;
it is likewise of the same class as the [visualization] sūtras. The Buddha-realm is sublime while the ordinary mind is coarse; it is difficult to achieve single-mindedness in three ways.
Contemplation requires leisure and ease, whereas diligent practice involves hardship and opposition; who would be willing to sit back and remain constant in their efforts?
Yet, as for the invocation of the six-character name, even a child three feet tall can accomplish it. This sutra specifically rescues the degenerate age—is this not more than mere coincidence?
Question: You speak of the "Opening of the Principle through Compassion" and the "Single Mind of Affairs.

Now, if one mind exhausts the principle and another mind engages in affairs, these two minds arise alternately like two pestles striking together, moving chaotically without ceasing; how can this be called "non-chaos"?

If the principle were identical to affairs and affairs were identical to the principle, such that that single mind is this very single mind, then one would simply employ a single mind. Is this not so?
What is wrong with this? The *Lishi* (Ritual for Paying Homage) states: "To manifest principle through phenomena is yet another method of contemplation.

It is not appropriate to speak of them as exclusively "contemplation of principle" or "contemplation of phenomena. Such is indeed the nature of the Tiantai teaching; since Ciyun was a successor to that tradition, how could he alone be otherwise?
Answer: Wisdom is one, yet it clarifies both the provisional and the real; it does not split wisdom to create duality.
Mind is one, yet it speaks of both the delusive and the true; it does not break the mind to make it two. When contemplating both phenomena and principle, what hindrance could there be?

It is like a mirror and its reflection, distinct yet inseparable; or water and the moon, divided yet uninterrupted. If one contemplates the principle through phenomena, the principle exists within phenomena. From...
If one investigates their affairs by reasoning through principle, affairs do not exist outside of principle; why, then, wait for thoughts to arise in two separate places?
Since the mallet and pestle are struck together in disarray, principle and affairs are one yet two, and two yet one; they are neither dissimilar nor estranged from one another.

Moreover, since it is said that "principle is revealed by means of affairs," they are of a single kind yet function as a dual pair—this clarity is indeed profound. Such is the case regarding Ciyun’s relation to the Tiantai teachings.
Furthermore, what is so contradictory about this?
Question: It seems that in the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is used as the cause for the Pure Land.

Previously, one doubted that [the Pure Land] being devoid of women and retinues would be insufficient to encourage ordinary beings; this was precisely because [the author] took what is impure to be pure. Now...
To thoroughly understand impurity and give rise to a mind of weary detachment—could this not be the true cause for the Pure Land?

However, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-śāstra* states that even when the contemplation of impurity is perfected, one has not yet escaped the three realms; this must mean that one only knows the impurity of the mundane world but does not yet know the impurity of the various heavens.
Even if one were able to thoroughly understand the impurity of the various heavens, would it not still be possible to be born in a pure land?
Answer: The Sahā world is impure, and women are but one aspect of that impurity. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* explains this impurity in detail, though its primary intent concerns women.
If one merely knows that impurity is to be loathed without aspiring toward the Pure Land, rebirth there will not be easy.

Even if the meditation on the skeleton (*asthi-bhāvanā*) is perfected, if one does not contemplate the Buddha’s body, it is difficult to ascend to the Land of Bliss. Thus, the contemplation of impurity serves as the very foundation for the Pure Land.
This is likely not the case. Question:
In the Pure Land, the water birds and forest trees expound upon the meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; this is surely not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Since that Buddha intends for the sound of the Dharma to flow forth, why does he not emit a single perfect sound (*ekadhvani*) to cause it?

If beings are delivered according to their respective types, why must it necessarily be this sound? Might it not be that, in order to gather those śrāvakas of fixed nature and cause them to come to this land, you have produced this sound again, so as not to allow their old afflictions to increase further?
Answer: The dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness are not limited or narrow. Indeed, they penetrate from the highest to the lowest; they are both partial and complete.
To observe that which is neither born nor extinguished is called impermanence; for the five aggregates not to arise is true suffering.
When Bodhisattvas hear this meaning, they further broaden their minds; when Śrāvakas understand this sound, they suddenly forget their smallness. Not so.
It is called the "Perfect Sound" (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*).
Why is this so? Question: Those dwelling within the lotus womb for six or twelve kalpas have not heard the Dharma preached by the Three Sages;
yet, within a distance of one *yojana*, there must be many water birds and forest trees. How is it that those inferior ordinary beings perceive only impermanence?

Regarding the meaning of suffering, emptiness, and non-self: one must not grasp at any of the forms and appearances before one's eyes. Once this non-grasping has persisted for a long time, they should naturally be extinguished.
How could the wheel of the chariot and the lotus-stalk remain alone? Furthermore, it is said that the pleasures of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are like this:
having already experienced such celestial bliss, how can one be certain of not falling back? Moreover, even when one does not fall, why not directly cultivate the path of this very heaven?
Is it karma? Answer:
That the lotus opens late in the evening is precisely because during one's life in the world, one did not realize the principles of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
Had one earlier clarified these principles, how could one have remained so long within the calyx of the lotus? Thus we know that by not grasping at form, one attains golden color.

When the flowers bloom, if one does not grasp at their marks, then the Buddha of Sublime Marks will appear; the Way of nurturing the lotus lies therein. What need is there for the doctrine of "dissolving the flowers"?

If one were to say that this bliss is comparable to that of the heavens, I fear it would lead to retrogression. One must understand that the use of the heavens as a metaphor is intended to show that those born in the Pure Land no longer feel longing or envy for celestial palaces;
thus, even while dwelling in bliss, they are not deluded. How could those whose resolve is set on the Great Way ever be content with such things?
They then cultivate celestial pleasures. Or again, it may be said that since their enjoyment is equal to that of the heavens above, how can their physical status be ranked as inferior?

This would precisely demonstrate that the three realms, though lofty, do not equal the nine lotuses below; for although their realization of the fruit is humble, the retribution they receive is already superior.
A crown prince, though still in swaddling clothes, is distinct from many officials; the kalaviṅka bird, before emerging from the womb, has a voice that surpasses all others.
Birds. Therefore, being reborn below is still superior to dwelling in celestial palaces; this ancient teaching is clear and manifest, leaving no room for further caviling.
Question: Humans fear that the matter of birth and death is great and that impermanence is swift; thus they first develop a fierce desire to seek liberation, not daring to rest for even a moment.
Yet, upon hearing the principle of transcending the triple world by a shortcut and the discourse on the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation)...
Regarding the texts for the eradication of sins and the ten recitations of the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land, people claim there is a Buddha upon whom to rely and no karma sufficient to fear;
thus they remain complacent and ultimately fail to gain efficacy, resulting in many falling into the hands of King Yama. This is because the Lotus School has led them astray.
Furthermore, the two approaches of the Chan and Teaching schools are extremely difficult to investigate and do not permit the swift realization of merit.
[The questioner] says: "How can these two words, 'birth' and 'death,' always be bound to one's mind? How could such a thing be possible? [The Master] answers:

"Among ordinary people who cultivate the Way, there are those who stop when they hear of difficulties and proceed when they hear of ease; there are also those who exert themselves when they hear of difficulties."

Those who hear of what is easy may become indolent; yet the ancient sages established their teachings each according to what was appropriate for the time. Whether one excels in applying the mind depends solely upon the individual.
This single path of reciting the Buddha’s name allows for direct transcendence of the three realms; it is the ultimate expression of great compassion that this gate was opened.

As for the failure to practice due to negligence and laxity, it is the sentient beings themselves who err—it is not the Buddha who errs regarding sentient beings. "If I desire benevolence, then benevolence... [will come].
This is the ultimate point. Benevolence is right before one's eyes; when the frantic mind can give rise to a single thought of mindfulness, sagehood is achieved.

That sagehood is not remote—does this not also make the Way too easy and thereby mislead people? As for the claim that a single word leads to sudden enlightenment and one becomes a Buddha on the spot, the Chan school’s assertion of ease goes even further than this.
How could such a thing also be called misleading?
Question: Fenggan was an emanation of Amitābha; Hanshan and Shide were Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Yet, when Amitābha appears, he does not lead with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, but instead wanders accompanied by Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Furthermore, his spoken words consist mostly of Chan (Zen) terminology.
Is it not the case that he regards the practices of *nienfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) and *guanfo* (contemplating the Buddha) as restrictive, and has thus shifted toward [the path of] suchness?
"Does this mean you have come to become a patriarch of Chan? Or are you one from the Land of Constant Quiescent Light? If it were not for such a person, there would be no way to receive me.
Answer: "It is well known that Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta constantly attend their Teacher; yet how could Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra ever have been separated from him for even a moment?"
Therefore, Śākyamuni is the transformation master of the Sahā world, yet Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara were present among his assembly;
Huangbo was not a patriarch of Confucianism, yet he hosted the Prime Minister Pei Xiu. How could there be any fixed rule in such matters of integrating and transforming beings through teaching?

As for the claim that discourse involving the Chan school seems to overturn pure karma—little do they realize that within each petal of the nine lotus blossoms, every branch unfolds the countenance of Kāśyapa, and the seven treasures...
The balustrades, step by step, lead one into the pavilion of Sudhana. Each of the eight facets of the ūrṇā-kośa reveals the true exposition of the Middle Way.

Each character of the six-syllable name demonstrates the esoteric intent of the West. There is no need to wait for the Small Vehicle to be transformed into the Great, or for the restricted to be changed into the universal, before receiving those of superior capacity and unfolding this profound transformation.
Thus we know that the single path of *nianfo* (buddha-recollection) is itself the entry [into the Dharma].
This wondrous gateway of principle perfectly accords with the five schools and extensively encompasses all teachings. Its subtlety is unfathomable; its vastness is boundless.
Those of dull faculties who obtain it will swiftly escape the wheel of suffering; those of sharp intelligence who encounter it will directly transcend to the other shore.
It appears coarse yet is subtle; it seems easy yet is difficult. May you all contemplate it deeply; be careful not to treat it with negligence.
